utterances.text: Before we go to these documents could you clarify one thing for me, please. Why do you say the use of the name Siptars was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because those Albanians thought it was a pejorative term to use. I had in mind their feelings rather than ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if -- yeah, do you see 6D666 on the screen? This is that document dated 3 April, it's an official note and it has the typewritten title and name of General Lukic. Is an official note the kind of thing that should have a signature in MUP documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I were asked the same way you put the question to me, then I would have answered that it may not have been approved by its authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I can understand how you might think a particular document may be authentic because it reflects other information you had -- I mean, it may reflect a conversation you had with somebody or a meeting you attended. And if it appears to be consistent, then that's one reason that you could think a document is authentic, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: Had I been asked about the document and whether I would believe the document to be authentic under the circumstances, then that would have presented a dilemma for me. That's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me present you a dilemma. Do you think this document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: If you compare this one with the Telefax message, which can be checked further because it was supposed to be coded, it has numbers, designators which can point you in a certain direction, then I would be more inclined to believe it is authentic than it is not. As I professional, I would have prefer to have this signed and then I could

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: understand that these were police documents drafted the police way. My suggestion was that before these are checked and verified as to their authenticity, that they were not to be used elsewhere. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Me too. I share some of your professional concerns. Let me ask you a series of questions about this particular document. When was the first time you saw this document, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 6D666, this official note dated 3 April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've already noted that this one has no signature and there's no stamp on the document. Some other documents we've seen in this case may have an archive stamp or they may have an army stamp or a Ministry of Defence stamp, but there's no stamp on this document either, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: The army was far more disciplined as compared to ourselves, if I may say so without it being held against me; but I don't think it was possible for the army to have something like this happen. Does this suffice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I -- first of all, I won't hold it against you. And is there -- but were there stamps used in the MUP on their documents at all or sometimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: I think that in the case of this document as well as many other documents from the staff we had a different situation that occurred. All those documents extracted from a computer had their originals which probably had been signed and approved, but the building had been bombed. And according to my information it was destroyed. Perhaps I spoke in jest when I said that the police was not in good in verifying as the

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that the original could be lost or destroyed in a bombing. First let me ask you about this particular document. Would this particular official note exist anywhere else other than at the MUP staff? Is it just an internal document made for their file or was this sent out to the SUP chiefs as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: No. This note when the order was being conveyed was drafted as evidence or corroboration to the person who can issue the order that this was indeed done. Then an extra effort was made and the order was sent via the Telefax message. When I compare the two I realize that it was one and the same thing, that is how I understood it. It didn't go to the chiefs of SUPs, but to the guy up there. And the Telefax message went to the chiefs of SUPs, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What's your -- what's the basis for your saying that this official note went to the guy up there? There's nothing on the document itself to suggest that. How do you assume that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: I presume so because this type of note -- well, I don't know who it went to, but this note is drafted only in the situation -- well, often you are found in a situation to convey other persons' orders and you have to do that even if you disagree with someone's order; however, you have to see it through. Then you can draft a note and send it to your superior so that you had to do something following somebody's order but

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: It was in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a series of questions from that answer. Let me start with your earlier answer where you said that you thought this official note a copy would have gone to the guy up there. Who did you have in mind when you were talking about the guy up there, some superior of Sreten Lukic I take it, but who in particular were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: I think that I said that it was my understanding that his superior could be the chief of sector or the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand the process right, this is something that you might do if you were in Sreten Lukic's place to show your boss: I've sent that message on, that order that came down for the SUP chiefs, I've got to sent it on. Is that right, just let the boss know that his message got out to the people it was supposed to go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: What I would like to add to that is that if it has to do with a serious matter, if -- it's not that somebody doesn't want to carry something out, but on the next day, for example, somebody may not comply with it, and I don't want to share the responsibility for that kind of thing. I think that that's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that makes sense to me. You said also I think regarding this document that you thought the date is wrong, the 3 April date probably should be 5 April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: Well, that's what the Defence attorney said. I just helped him in terms of his assumption to bring it into a zone of probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But in terms of zone of probability, just looking at this document there's really no -- there's really no way we can know when it was created, right? It says 3 April 1999, but it could have been typed up 3 April 2002, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: The 3rd of April, 2002? Just a moment. Let me consult the documents, I really have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: The questions are very serious. First of all, let me say that we are dealing with documents that are unsigned, that have not been authorised, so we are in the sphere of assumptions. Let me just find the Telex. It was a day earlier or a day later in relation to the note, the 15th of April, the Telex, that's when it left, the meeting was on the 4th. It's possible. You know, it's possible that a mistake happened -- a typographical error. There is no reason for me to be suspicious, just an ordinary mistake, a typo, there's no reason for me to think it was typed in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But right now I'm just talking in general terms about authenticity of documents in general, and if you have an unsigned typewritten document with no stamp on it and not being able to do some kind of forensic examination about, you know, when the paper was created or when this particular type of ink was first in use or when this type of printer existed, you and I looking at it don't know when this was created, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: Precisely, but the question is that if we want to find out then we can go through the documents and try to link them up with something that is truthful; namely, that the meeting took place, that a Telex was sent with that content. And then if we so wish sincerely, to place that on the same plain with that and say, Well, yes, it's possible that it was a technical error, wartime conditions, you know the building was destroyed, notes are being typed up elsewhere, there's no electricity, and so on and so forth, not to go into all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see this particular one is in Latin script rather than Cyrillic. Was there a common practice in the MUP in 1998 and 1999 regarding the use of Latin versus Cyrillic script or were they used equally depending on who was doing the writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: that's in the Latin script as well. That is my only comment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 6D-2
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it seems to prevail. But we who lived in Kosovo and worked there had to know Albanian too, and then perhaps we were more inclined to use the Latin script because it's more practical for typing purposes and generally speaking. The Cyrillic script is a bit more complex as an alphabet I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Then could we look -- well, maybe I'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to go to another document. I wonder if we could recess for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I might be able to finish in one session tomorrow, the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Is the expert witness also yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stamp will be cross-examining that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he's had time to work on his preparation while this is happening?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he's had more time than I have, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apart from Mr. Simonovic, what other treats do you have in store for us this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For this week, I don't think that we have anything unless the judge makes it, for example, on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's still a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is still possible, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very thin possibility. And I was just informed that most likely she would be here on Friday, Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And able to be led on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If they come here, they don't come that early to be able to participate in the court at all. So probably we will use

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was just going to say if she was intended to be led as a witness this week and there's a 92 ter statement we would request it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think we would be able to compose one because of that late arrival. Your Honour, if I may just add one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was only yesterday that we successfully persuaded her to come at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we have to conclude our hearing for today at this stage and resume tomorrow, that means that you will have to come back here to complete your evidence, and that will be tomorrow morning at 9.00. Between now and then it's vital that you should have no communication whatsoever with anyone about any aspect of the evidence in this case. Please bear that in mind. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher and return here at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.31 p.m.,
